blocks.text: Imagine your computer as a busy office manager. How does it efficiently handle multiple tasks like printing, reading from a disk, and displaying graphics without getting overwhelmed?

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore how operating systems manage input/output (I/O) operations. We will delve into the mechanisms of polling, interrupts, and direct memory access (DMA), and understand the critical role of device drivers in the I/O stack.

blocks.title: Polling
blocks.text: Polling is a technique where the CPU repeatedly checks the status of an I/O device to see if it needs attention.

blocks.markdown: Polling is straightforward but can be inefficient. The CPU continuously checks the device status, which can waste CPU cycles if the device is not ready.

blocks.title: Interrupt-Driven I/O
blocks.text: Interrupt-driven I/O allows devices to signal the CPU when they are ready for data transfer, freeing the CPU to perform other tasks in the meantime.

blocks.markdown: Interrupts improve efficiency by allowing the CPU to execute other instructions until the device is ready. When the device signals an interrupt, the CPU pauses its current task to handle the I/O operation.

blocks.title: Polling vs Interrupt-Driven I/O
blocks.prompt: Consider a scenario where a CPU must read data from a keyboard. Compare how polling and interrupt-driven I/O handle this task.

steps.text: In polling, the CPU continuously checks the keyboard's status register to see if a key has been pressed.
In interrupt-driven I/O, the keyboard sends an interrupt signal to the CPU when a key is pressed, allowing the CPU to handle other tasks until the interrupt occurs.

blocks.answer: Interrupt-driven I/O is more efficient as it allows the CPU to perform other tasks while waiting for the keyboard input.

blocks.title: Direct Memory Access (DMA)
blocks.text: DMA is a feature that allows I/O devices to send or receive data directly to or from the main memory without continuous CPU intervention.

blocks.markdown: DMA reduces CPU involvement by allowing data transfers to occur directly between I/O devices and memory. The CPU is only involved at the beginning and end of the transfer.

blocks.title: Role of DMA
blocks.prompt: Explain how DMA improves system performance during a disk read operation.

steps.text: The CPU initiates the disk read operation by setting up the DMA controller with the memory address and size of the data to be transferred.
The DMA controller manages the data transfer directly between the disk and memory, freeing the CPU to perform other tasks.

blocks.answer: DMA improves performance by offloading the data transfer task from the CPU, allowing it to execute other instructions concurrently.

blocks.title: Device Driver
blocks.text: A device driver is a specialized software component that allows the operating system to communicate with hardware devices.

blocks.markdown: Device drivers act as translators between the operating system and hardware devices, converting OS commands into device-specific actions.

blocks.title: Key Point
blocks.text: Efficient I/O management is crucial for system performance, as it allows the CPU to focus on processing tasks rather than managing data transfers.

points: Polling involves the CPU actively checking device status, which can be inefficient.
Interrupt-driven I/O allows devices to notify the CPU when they are ready, improving efficiency.
DMA enables direct data transfers between devices and memory, reducing CPU involvement.
Device drivers facilitate communication between the OS and hardware devices.
